[h1]What goes around comes around...[/h1]

Indie horror market was rich in production for the last couple of years, and [i]DISTRAINT[/i] was among its presents to us lucky horror gamers. As being Jesse Makkonen's second game so far - yup, a one man made wonder here - it's been completed in 3 months as a challenge. With this astounding time and labor limit, I must say that the result is praiseworthy. The game is short, strikingly disturbing and symbolic with a plot so ordinary, you'd wonder how it came to be found worthy enough to tell as a story. Yet, this simplicity bears the beauty of it all. I personally enjoyed every second of it, and would gladly recommend taking on this 2 hours journey, if you enjoy horror settings and subconscious symbolisms.

The name of the game comes to be quite self-explanatory actually. You play as a young and ambitious man named Price, who has been trying to gain partnership from a famous company. He is not a bad guy really, but he bears the burden of choosing one of the least favorable career paths known to humanity: poor little Price is a sequestrator, and he is responsible of seizing people's properties when they cannot pay their debts. As the game starts, our first task is to distrain an old lady's home. Since Mrs. Goodwin's husband is long dead, and she doesn't have much favorable assets in the pragmatic sense, a heartbreaking end awaits her, and poor little Price is tasked with arranging that end. The moment he delivers the news, his guilt begins to take root and this guilt starts to manifest as strikingly gruesome hallucinations. As the game progresses, Price realizes that he indeed sold his humanity rather cheap.

Now this game has been somewhat criticized in the community, that collecting debts shouldn't be considered evil since it’s just a job, you know, not the mother of all evil. Thus, business shouldn't be the cause of guilt and a crippled conscience. Right? Now, this is an ethical debate and it is the exact kind of question this game wishes for you to ask yourselves. This context of business is the perfect cover for the proverbial elephant in the room: - which you'll literally encounter more than once in the game - if a deed could be pragmatically indorsed and lawfully justified at the same time, the substance of the action or its end result doesn't reach our conscience. Business is business nonetheless. The narrative and symbolism within the game are quite basic, simplistic even. Yet, they criticize this specific self-justification very successfully. If an action is deemed just, it doesn't also necessarily be considered good or kind.

For a 2D scroller horror adventure, character and environment design within the game are really well elaborated. There is a certain sense of desolateness in all places, a neglect and a darkness. Subtle symbolisms of small sceneries are well-woven. Cute, bubble headed character designs used in especially gory displays throughout the game really startle you. As another huge display quality, both the soundtrack and the sound effects are masterfully arranged and utilized to enhance the atmosphere furthermore, even inducing a couple jump scares. The game pace is a mostly low growing adventure, with simple puzzles and a couple of timing actions with no actual threat to you character at all. The whole experience wraps up within 2 hours, and casual [i]Twin Peaks[/i] references are a nice bonus.

Now that [i]DISTRAINT 2[/i] is already announced to come for this winter, I can sincerely recommend this short experience for a silent night. It might be considered a bit expensive for the full price, with this short of a completion time, so the next sale would be as grand as any to try. I congratulate Jessi Makkonen to go under this feat and present us the subconscious of poor little Price. Enjoy!

Look, I've played my fair share of retro 2D style, pixel graphics-esque indie horror games like Lone Survivor, The Final Station, Claire, Uncanny Valley, Home, Reveal the Deep, Settled, The Last Door, etc.

Distraint… doesn’t live up to the “Overwhelmingly Positive” review. I have no qualms about the graphics, sound, atmosphere, or puzzles—they were decent. 

My issue with this game was THE PLOT. The plot was laughably cliché, the characters were one-dimensional caricatures with no emotional depth, and the symbolism was heavyfisted.

Stories that focus on the protagonist’s guilt and horrific manifestations of said guilt actually require the protagonist to have actually DONE something guilt-worthy. Like killing their wife. Stealing from an elderly couple in order to survive only to find that they have died of starvation the next day.

… Working for the IRS doesn’t constitute as a soul-crushingly guilty action. It’s a JOB.

If my landlord kicks me out because I can’t pay the rent, is he a morally-deprived landlord? Hell no, it’s just business.

Same logic applies in this game. Just because Price is the harbinger of bad news doesn’t mean he has to shoulder the personal burden of evicting the residents out of their apartments to the point where blood-smeared elephants are chasing him through endless hallways.

The moral of this game is that GREED = BAD. Yet Price wasn’t greedy—he was trying to make a decent living. He’s clearly very poor, judging from the decrepit state of his apartment from the ruined kitchen to the leaks in his ceiling. His parents are dead, despite the fact Price is in his 20-30’s. He’s an underdog, trying to survive in a tough world—and he immediately gets lambasted for pursuing the most unpopular career known to mankind. Sorry, but someone has to do it.

First off, I wanna say, props to Jesse for putting this together in 3 months.  It's obvious a lot of work went into the game, and it's awesome that he was able to get it completed.  

This game is, artistically, beautiful.  I absolutely HATE retro graphic, 2D side scrollers, but this one really changed my mind.  The music and sound effects were amazing, the characters were well drawn and had neat swaying motions.  The game looks nice.  

But it does not play nice.  No, no.  This game is slow and a snooze-fest.  The 'puzzles' aren't puzzles.  You walk from point A to point B to point C, back to point B, and then maybe over to point D.  There isn't really a whole lot of logic involved in these puzzles.  The hitboxes for selection can also be wonky at times, so you can easily skip over certain action items.  Act 3, I had to actually use a guide, since there is no map/point of reference to where you've been.  You just wander aimlessly and go down a memory checklist, hoping you are going in the correct direction.  

Price also moves at a snail's pace.  It's fine at first, because you get to see the art, but during segments like I have described above, it makes the game about twice as long as it needs to be (my playtime was idle, I spent an hour 15 actually playing).  It just gets dull, and the story needs to move along.  

The writing is absolutely horrendous.  The other negative reviewers hit the nail on the head.  The story reads like an edgy highschooler's emo diary.  It's trying to make some deep statement against 'the man' and how debt collection is somehow inherently evil (???).  Isn't it just as evil to NOT pay your debts?  Yea, moral relativism is a pain, I know.  

Also, it seems that Jesse couldn't decide on a tone for the game.  Price goes from "I'm so sorry madam..." and "I'm an evil whippersnapper" to "[Expletive]!" "[Expletive]!" "[Expletive]!" at random times.  It is just all over the place.  There are weird drug-induced mushroom castles one moment and blood covered walls the next.  I did like the creepy ambiance that the game provided though, I am not a big horror buff, so I did jump a few times.  

All this said, the game was 99 cents, and it WAS an experience.  I do not believe that it is a good game, by any definition of the word, and the Overwhelmingly Positive review is mind boggling to me.  If you wanna blow an hour and play a poorly written, yet pretty game, then DISTRAINT is for you.  

I do not regret purchasing it.  However, I do not feel like I would recommend it.

Edit:  Removed unnecessary vitriol towards people who did enjoy the game.

[h1]What Comes Around, Goes Around[/h1]

Distraint is a bit-sized 2D psychological-horror game from Finnish developer Jesse Makkonen now re-released with new color palette, enhanced animation and lighting. The story is about an ambitious young man named Price who happens to be just an ordinary guy working for a greedy company that seizes people’s property. In exchange for a partnership with his employers Price is sent to meet with three people who he must inform can no longer stay in their home. 

Price is portrayed as a genuinely good guy who just wants to live a normal life. He isn't chasing after exorbitant riches; All he wants is a home that doesn't leak in rainy days but at what cost? As the story progresses he can feel that his humanity is gone, so the rest of his journey follows him dealing with himself and his choices along the way. His basic desires, rather than a hyperbolic chasing of wealth, shift the game to a neutral perspective that allow you to sympathize with both Price and the victims of his line of work. In conclusion the story is about "regrets".

The gameplay is kept simplistic but very effective and that works. Most of the time you would find items and solve simple puzzles. Creative mix of artistic design, sound with pixelated horror effects makes Distraint a very unique experience. The soundtrack is yet again very beautiful and just feels natural given the game's tone and the stuff you see in the game! I gotta appreciate that the entire game was crafted by one guy and that's pretty impressive and puts other games from similar genre to shame. Distraint's story is twisted but the developer also delivers positive [and negative] messages but how you take it is left upto you.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
-Skillfully told story that's very engaging and touching
-Good use of dark humor 
-Soundtrack that just works really well...
-Perfect balance of creepy atmosphere and some refreshing moments that'll keep you engaged with the 2 hour adventure
-Compelling premise of self-destructive regrets
-satisfying ending (wished if there were multiple endings)

[h1]Cons[/h1]
-No interactive dialogues 
-Some grammer mistakes due to poor translation
-No way to rebind keys or change graphical settings
-A bit too short

[h1] My Rating: 8/10 [/h1]

I bought it on sale and it was worth every penny. The duration of the game and the sale price of the game kinda balance themselves out in that aspect I suppose. It's on sale frequent number of times, so yes I recommend; do buy it. Distraint is a damn fine horror game which will keep you hooked with Price's adventures.

In one word, [i]DISTRAINT[/i] is "inconsistent".

[h1]Foreword[/h1]
This review contains [b]mild spoilers[/b] since this title's weaker points, those I chastise the most throughout the review, are plot-related. Crucial aspects of the plot, however, are [b]not[/b] disclosed in this review.

[h1]General impressions[/h1]
I feel it is important to open this review by saying that by no stretch of the mind did [i]DISTRAINT[/i] live up to its "overwhelmingly positive" status. I also feel like this is one of those reasonably good, short, often discounted — and therefore cheap — titles that, for those reasons alone, attract a barrage of people that find no imminent reason to give it a thumbs down but instead find easy means of writing a two line review giving it a thumbs up.

It is a ridiculously easy task to recommend [i]DISTRAINT[/i] by means of a single paragraph review praising Jesse for his one-man handiwork, artistic skills and creativity. It is, however, much more taxing to look past that mask of success and into the misery that must be the life of a badly scripted businessman who can't decide between good, wrong, insanity and sanity and, for the love of me, seems to live in world where every evicted place reeks of a profound degradation, much like his own home.

[h1]Where it succeeds[/h1]
[b]The art[/b] of [i]DISTRAINT[/i] is one that catches the eye even of those who do not normally appreciate pixel art. It is expressive and helps set the sad and hopeless atmosphere presented throughout the game.

[b]The premise[/b] is one hardly seen anywhere else. A video game played in the shoes of a businessman had everything to turn out terribly due to its similarities with real life, but Jess put it all fearlessly on the table without making players flinch away.

[b]The music[/b], although not particularly noteworthy, works to the game's benefit and its attempt at an atmosphere, rather than against it.

[h1]Where it tumbles[/h1]
[b]The script[/b], even if not ridden with typos, is weak and inconsistent. Be it Price, Price's parents, Price's managers or the evictees, [i]DISTRAINT[/i] wobbles between their facades as though it wasn't too sure about its own characters. The disharmony in Price's personality does not translate to the player by means of conflicted writing, but instead by writing conflicts. The final straw of that is Price's final decision, which is as predictable as it is final towards completely snuffing out what could have been a brilliant character progression or, perhaps, a light of hope. 

[b]The puzzles[/b] are as weak as they come as they resort to timing, trial and error (with much grunting involved), and even a terrible word puzzle.

[b]The level design[/b] was the source of many difficulties through the game. Sometimes the only thing that made getting from point A to point B taxing was how awfully designed the levels were. They included, but were not limited to: getting off the path or playing longer sequences just to save the game, going round and round due to missing a door by 5 second since Price's mysterious "narcotic" wore out (I'm referring to the third distraint, the worst of them all in every single aspect), having to stand at a [b]precise[/b] spot facing the right direction in order to interact with people or things, walking in pitch-black darkness, having to randomly guess the order to do things despite no indication of so and, finally, an inconsistent difficulty balance. I could go on, but these annoyed me the most.

[b]The horror[/b] is not psychological, is not jump-scary and is most definitely not built around an atmosphere. The horror is just straight-up [b]weak[/b]. Sometimes it was gore-related — cannibalism is one example and a Fargo-inspired scene another —, sometimes it took the form of something that moved in the corner of your eye, sometimes it was just a random explosion of sound. During all those instances, my blank expression persisted and my nostalgia of atmospheric games grew ever stronger.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
[b]"Inconsistent"[/b] is my word of choice for [i]DISTRAINT[/i] because even its tiny details do not add up. Price's madness is selective, people hide passwords behind word puzzles — and this is [b]not[/b] Puzzle Agent! —, an elderly woman attempts breaking into a cemetery with a crowbar that you then proceed to steal from her in order to break into a man's backyard while you are trying to seek redemption for your bad deeds, a nursery home is worse than the worst real-life nursery homes just because it [b]can[/b] be, and there is absolutely no reason, by end-game, to care about any of the characters so shallowly presented.

Perhaps [i]DISTRAINT[/i]'s biggest inconsistency is feasting on the assumption that everyone who evicts anyone for a living is, by consequence, trying to copulate with Satan due to greed. Yes, even when that means finally getting the funds for a morning coffee.

Distraint is a 2D psychological horror game that displays a lot of creative value. The game drifts a little permissive between reality and unreality, but the presentation evokes an effectively peculiar and unsettling atmosphere, and solely improved by the exceptional sound design. Distraint rarely leans on cheap jump scares, opting instead for a slow-burning horror to establish a feeling of anxiety. The gameplay is simple and fairly minimal, and the puzzles provides just enough substance to carry through to its dramatic conclusion. Distraint is surely not a protracted game, but it has a captivating and unique story about greed.

Since playing the “Devil Went Through Here” series, I’ve sort of fallen in love with the horror-adventure genre and I’m happy to report that this game has only added fuel to the fire.

Before I get ahead of myself, I should address the elephant in the room: I’m not sure I understand the artistic direction, here. Like, why do all the characters look like toddlers wearing poopy diapers? Maybe there’s something deeper, here… Perhaps it’s a comment on the infantile, self-interested nature of greed? Maybe it’s a reflection of Price’s childlike hero-worship directed toward the heads of the firm where he works and his attempt to grow and gain power in a world that tends to regard him as meek and inconsequential? I don’t have a clue. It kind of just looks like everyone in the game shit their pants. Whatever.

Aside from the weirdness, [i]Distraint[/i] proved to be a solid experience. While it curated some moments that will haunt me for a long time, for sure, it also knew how to be fun. (Throwing a drug-fueled eviction party for a soon-to-be homeless renter comes to mind.)

The story was somewhat simplistic but still thought-provoking. I mean, I never thought I’d play a horror game about bankers or whatever, so I have no standard to measure it against. It still freaked me out, that’s for sure: by the end, I was filled with a sense of dread because I knew that that if I was in the same situations as Price, I’d probably wind up doing the same fucking thing.

And that’s the reason I have to recommend this one: the kind of horror that makes me look inward and examine myself is exactly the kind of horror I strive to find. So, if you’re in the market for a horror story with a unique premise and are willing to make allowances for an… interesting… art style, you can’t go wrong with this one. I am personally excited to see what [i]Distraint 2[/i] has in store.

Distraint is a good example of a classic indie game, that was created first and foremost for the sake of the story which the author wanted to share with everyone. It combines a bit of a direct narrative, a bit of environmental storytelling and some atmospheric sound design to deliver its message.

The message in question in this kind of games games is a highly subjective thing, and if you're interested in the game, you better make your own opinion of it, but my version comes under the spoiler: [spoiler] People ruin lives of other people for what appears a considerable wealth to them, when in reality it's more like 2 cents. They're not making their lives better, as making the lives of everyone around worse, which is why everything declines.[/spoiler]

Distraint has a sound story, not those pretentious "boy longes for a girl in a platformer game" setups you see these days. And because this game is a one man effort, its every component (be it graphics, puzzles, sound, or visual effects) is really consistent with the storytelling, providing a very solid overall experience.

Technically, this game is a 2D adventure with a dystopic setting and lots of horror elements.
The game has 4 main levels (based on story arcs), with an addition of several smaller levels made for the sake of artistic exposition. Don't worry, though, Distraint is not a walking simulator - you'll have to solve multiple puzzles to progress through each of the main stages. There is also a nice degree of funny interactions you can make by applying items from your inventory to unexpected targets. After each story arc is done, you return to the protagonist's apartments to wrap things up.

Speaking of the horror elements, they are made not so much to scare you, as to make an accent on some point of the story or develop a charachter trait. Overall, it works well, the game doesn't create suspense, but rather a feeling of phantasmagoria, and does it quite elaborately, so it doesn't fall apart as a bunch of random nonsense. Also, the game has some really good findings in horror department. [spoiler]THERE IS AN ELEPHANT IN THE ROOM[/spoiler]

Even though Distraint has a relatively slow pace, it really makes you wonder what will happen next. And what happens next really can come off as a surprise - or as a deppressingly accurate prediction.

Currently, SteamSpy estimates Distraint to have around 32k owners, and it definetly deserves more attention. If you miss the feeling of the game made by a single author, you should definetly play Distraint.

Distrainor, is a person, who comes to you in the most unsuitable times. When you are full of debts, problems, life issues and other not so pleasant stuff. His job is pretty much simple - to inform you that you need to move out of your apartment/house/whatever by the end of the month. Reasons can vary - from the inability to pay its rent to the government’s need of this territory for some other construction, for example shopping mall or highway project. 

There is a trick about this profession - you have to be a cold heart person, who doesn’t care about anyone and human’s feeling is not a thing for you. Because, no surprise, that when you will come to the place to distrain you will see tears, pain, despair in the owner’s eyes, begging you to give them one more chance. In this case, all you have to do is remain heartless and stay on your own - either you move out or you gonna face real problems, you don’t wanna face with!

This game tells you a story about a distrainor, who lives in a bad apartment full of issues and holes in the roof. His main objective is to become successful to live in a better place, have a better salary and become a partner in his evil company. On his road to this goal he won’t stop at anything so he moves to his next assignment. When he arrives he sees a creepy halls full of dirty apartments and its owners, the whole atmosphere is damn scary and makes you feel uncomfortable. You crawl through this hall full of evil dwellers until you find the right person - old granny, who has nothing left in her life except this apartment and now she is going to lose this one as well. Good news, is that she is not stupid and she understands that you only do your job and you would be more than happy for her to stay there, but you are afraid that this is impossible. After informing her, you leave this creepy place, which is followed by the horror cutscene and from this moment, our protagonist starts to feel guilty and he begins to understand that his job is nothing more than a dirty game of a greedy, dirty, heartless fat bureaucratic pigs, who only care about money and power. 

However, Price is not the same person. At least, he thinks so. Through the whole game, he has this unstoppable battle inside of himself, trying to understand who he really is. On one hand he has this feeling, that he does something wrong and that this poor old lady will be left behind somewhere on the streets without a roof upon her head. This feeling becomes worse, when he sees this creepy horror visions and he starts to see his dead parents, which are trying to appeal to Price’s compassion. But on the other hand, he still lives in this poor apartment, which state is really miserable and he can’t wait to move out of that place ASAP. So, when it comes to simple question either I recommend this game or not, I can be put in a tricky situation, because I don’t have a one solid question. DISTRAINT is a 2D point and click adventure wherein you have to do your normal point and click stuff - go talk to people, interact with the environment, and solve puzzles. It's all done in a mostly fluid way, though I found a puzzle with mushrooms towards the end to be a particularly tough challenge of one's reflexes, when combined with a bit of pixel hunting to actually figure out where to go. But overall, the gameplay, while treading the well-worn path of countless adventure games that have come before it, is good. 

It's the story that adventure games are known for, and as mentioned before, DISTRAINT tells a bleak and oftentimes too-grim-to-stomach adventure. There are a few moments of levity, and some sweet or uplifting moments, but overall the tone of the game is dark and depressing. There's absolutely nothing wrong with this, and I genuinely enjoyed the story, but sometimes it all just got a bit too much. Perhaps it was what I was feeling when I played it a while back, but it really is a toughie, for all the good character writing and emotional moments it offers. I'll have to check out the sequel sometime, as I enjoyed this one enough to recommend it to others. 

It's not revolutionary, nor is it the most well-crafted adventure game you've ever played. But, if you're after a dark puzzler, this is the one for you.

[h1]"Paid My Dues"[/h1]

[u]The Gist:[/u]
Price is a debt collector who isn't doing the best financially. So, in an attempt to not pass up a rags-to-riches offer of making partner with McDade, Burton and Moore- he agrees to some legally but not morally justified decisions by evicting three individuals. However, he may not be as resilient as he thought because his actions begin to torment him slowly at first.... but surely. Can he go through with it after all? 

[spoiler] ! Last notice. You've been warned. [/spoiler]


[h1][+] PROS;[/h1]

[b](a) The Descent[/b]
Gameplay consists of 2D exploration and puzzle-solving, nothing too complex usually for a key item to unlock the next area or meet up with someone. Pick up an item, store it and then use it on another point of interest. If it sounds extremely simple, that's because it is which is a good thing! There is not even a button to run! Therefore, the controls are easy to master and don't distract you from being immersed in the well-crafted story, disturbing experiences as well as hopefully being able to take away the central lesson. 

Initially the game my seem cut-and-dry as it starts you off right away in the first distraint scenario and then plagued by the guilt shortly after. Then you return to your dwellings to start the next case. But you'll be surprised to hear it has a reasonable pace!

[b](b) A Deadly Sin[/b] 
I thought the plot was the strongest part of the game. Price is not actually a bad person, not at all instead he's just doing his job or so he tries to tell himself. Seeing him bothered by how the eviction affected the three very different individuals showed his treatment of others is still very humane. This is also apparent in how he tries to make the process as smooth and considerate as possible by fulfilling their requests. Some took more of a toll on him than others, particularly the elderly woman in poor health.

[spoiler]She could also technically be considered as the main "antagonist" because she's the source of his nightmares.[/spoiler] However, that would be presumptuous of me because after all Price brought it on himself and he has been shown to be rather materialistic as well by opting to get things like a new coffee maker and fantasizing of a better place, as is the aim of life after all.

[b](c) Shred of Sanity[/b] 
The game has a dark sense of humor and you often question whether it's appropriate to burst out laughing but then you do it anyways. There are many instances where you can "pretend" to match an obviously wrong item during your interactions which will actually hint at Price's defining trait- the ability to crack a joke and laugh at himself, the situation or both! These also nab you achievements and are just some harmless fun~ 

There also some rarer 4th wall-breaking dialogue such as when you save your progress which only make you realize this is a game based on reality. Then it sets in- how the game makes you take delight in every moment. Price's bosses encouraging him to do a celebratory dance is a small sign of control and priming him to take pleasure in the work.    

[b](d) Looking Out for No. 1[/b] 
I've probably touched on some of the horror elements; its close to home topic of debt, greed and what it can unleash. Now we'll explore more on what makes this scary. 

1st) The graphics- the grainy filter and design of the characters make them out to look barely human. This suits the central idea of Price selling himself for a chance at the grand life. For example, whether the grotesque and gory happenings that occur are real or has Price gone mad beyond saving? These hallucinations, nightmares although unnerving on their own; the often unknown sounds and excessively off-putting visuals. All these can be [spoiler]said to be symptoms of a mental illness playing out in extreme forms.[/spoiler] 

2nd) One section where he dabbles in an unknown substance to overcome obstacles as part of a puzzle subtly alluding to drugs of which is another indulgence he may well end up doing to ease his pain.

3rd) [Spoiler] There's also the fact that regardless of how badly you want to have a say in Price's choices and affect the outcome, you'll find it's impossible and you have to bear witness to what unfolds[/spoiler]. Case in point, the ending which is a real downer and I'd be lying if I said it didn't make me self-reflect.


[h1][-] CONS;[/h1]

[b](i) Not of Sound Mind[/b] 
I did encounter one interaction issue where the prompt to interact appears but is untouchable as if no description was written to begin with. However, perhaps most irritating is the slight delay or inconsistent near unpredictable nature of the prompt appearing when trying to examine stuff/people. When moving, the prompt doesn't appear- that's fine. So just stop right?

 But then you can only interact with them when facing at the right direction (often only one fixed one). It gets worse during one timed sequences! Of course, there's also how sometimes you can interact from an arm length's away and then others breathing down their necks. 

[b](ii) You'll Live[/b]
I mentioned that the puzzles are straightforward but they required quite a bit of backtracking, I'm sorry "backwalking" for such a linear game. I also had times where I went "huh" at the logic of some puzzles. I get that the world, his mental state become questionable and so this is mirrored in the puzzles. Still weird though... 

The scares also rely more on shock value and may have been a tad too violent, dare I say to the point of player desensitization. Unless, that was the point... There was one other baffling encounter where the same jumpscares were done twice in exactly the same way and it really bugged me.


[h1]"But Not The Price?"[/h1]

To conclude, Distraint is an exceptional 2D horror adventure that easily stands out with its scarring premise and very realistic portrayal of how greed can lead to one's spiral of regret. It poses a genuine dilemma that's still relevant- whether a person is ever truly sure of the difference between want and need. The despicable decisions that Price (or rather you) resorts to and the horrid episodes to punish you remain the most iconic scenes.

Distraint is a short psychological horror title in which you play the role of Price, a young man whose job is to seize the property of others. He quickly discovers that he's entering a decent paying career at the cost of his own humanity.

The game is full of hidden meanings (even Price's name), and the story is something that almost everyone who has had a job can relate to. Myself personally being a slave to call center careers for the past decade, I certainly know how the protagonist feels and the story really hits home for me. The graphics and gameplay style will easily remind players of titles such as Lone Survivor, Claire and Home. However, Distraint has a personality and concept that is unique to itself. The atmosphere in the game is heavy, brought on by dimly lit corridors and a pressurized ambiance that gives an overflowing sense of dread for the entirety of the game.

Distraint is an outstanding indie horror title that does its job of instilling fear and dread into the player. The puzzles are very easy and the game is very short, your initial playthrough may take anywhere from 1-2 hours to complete. Subsequent playthroughs will see 30-45 minute timeframes. There are a few grammatical errors within the dialogue at times, but the game is bug and crash free. 

The price has dropped significantly since launch, and Distraint is worth every penny of the $5.49 CAD asking price; it even goes on sale for $1.09 quite regularly. Additionally, it's very impressive that one person created this game in a little less than 3 months; the same creator behind Silence of the Sleep. If you're looking for a good horror title to spend some time with this Halloween or cold winter season, look no further.

Distraint is a beautiful pixel experience among indie psychological games. I first played it on Android and now on PC. And I have to admit that the Steam Deluxe Edition, with its colourful elements, is fantastic, unlike its standard counterpart.

Now for the overall gameplay experience:

You play as Price, a young man who tells his story of regret for his 'ambitious' choices. Here, the player can reflect on Price's actions. Was what happened in the story a natural consequence of his own emotional immaturity and the choices of the tenants he influenced? Was it the system that was ultimately evil, playing with people's destinies? Or was it the businessmen, always obsessed with ambition, who acted in the name of 'the law'?
Or was it a combination of factors, where no one is really black and white, but morally grey?
The developer obviously wanted to make a critique of the capitalist system, but also connect it to a deeper level. There are a lot of interesting scenes where the dev shows how corrupt the system is, but also how impressionable and childish Price is to a certain extent.
Now, I don't agree with many of Price's perceptions and some of his actions, but I also don't agree with some of the moral messages that the game tries to give us.

Ultimately, the game is open to interpretation, and it's a nice opportunity to reflect on our society and its flaws.

As for the horror part, I was expecting some mild horror, probably in the style of Mad Father or a similar title. The bobble head characters definitely remind me of Dead Road to Canada, very funny like.
What distinguishes Distraint is the constant fog-like atmosphere, the eerie music and the background effects, the latter of which keep you in suspense. The way you have to move around the rooms can also add to the tension. The whole story seems to be the product of a nightmare projected onto an old film.
It's a very curated way of presenting horror in pixels. There are a few references to sayings that come to life as part of Price's hallucinations, and because the theme remains a social and serious one, the game remains engaging for the most part.

I conclusion. Do I recommend it?
For the most part, yes. I do. It's a nice little game, don't expect it to be Silent Hill in pixels, this is an indie Game, and a short one. But it's worth the try, for what it offers. If you enjoy story rich games and your system hasn't the specs for a heavy horror game, this is a good option for a mildly chilling experience.

Fun little horror side scroller.

The game is meant to be a message about disregarding morals and the consequences of doing so. The obvious flaw is the fact that Price's actions were never immoral in the first place, nor is his story a good example of the aforementioned message.

Besides, Price's worries seem... greatly exaggerated, to say the least. I don't think that evicting a single person from their house would result in bloody, borderline insane delusions filled with gore and cannibalism. I mean, what? From the moment that started, it felt more like a reason to slap the "Psychological Horror" tag on the store page than an actual attempt of expressing Price's (unreasonable) guilt. It seemed pointless and forced.

The characters are either extremely shallow or the textbook definitions of good or evil with little to no in between. Gameplay wise, it leaves quite a bit to be desired - most of it is going from point A to B, looping back to A to find a path to C and so on. The mushroom level was a slog.

The artstyle and sound design are definitely the game's strong suits, though - they're unique, and added to the gloomy atmosphere throughout the game.

In short: Good idea, poor execution.

Distraint is 2D, pixel art, psychological thriller game about guilt, consciousness and regret. It also explores — little to the face of the player in my taste — consequences of greed and selling souls to corporations. And, yeah, I guess? Greed is bad. Those who understand this, don’t need to be educated about it. Those who embrace it, don't care and will not change their behaviour. You don’t need to have a big brain to understand it. Thankfully, instead of preaching, the game tries to tell something about the mental state of the person who experiences immense psychological pressure due to acting against their consciousness and beliefs. There is no redemption, no good ending, no “well done, you won”. Yeah, this game was done by Scandinavians. 

The game tries to be unsettling and spooky sometimes, but it is a little above mediocre in this department. You know, the standard package — flashing lights, moving shadows, loud, obnoxious sounds, all that jazz. Sometimes it works, sometimes not — well, maybe it’s because of me, I got fried in my horror circuits a long ago…

The thing is — there is not enough here. The game is very, very short — like maybe you need little more than 1,5 hours to finish it — also very light on puzzles; mostly talking NPC and using items on objects. There is one confusing mechanic in the later part, when you need to use psychedelic mushrooms to travel through dilapidated apartments, but aside that, nothing more sophisticated or deep. The story is galloping and does not have enough space to breathe to be some kind of “experience”. You rather get in, explore the game, and get out. I would prefer if this was a longer game with deeper dive to presented themes, but oh well, we got what we got — a game trying to tell some type of story without any kind of replayability.  

Now. It's over. Go home or something.

Basically Distraint is an indie 2D horror game where the 'horror' aspect is mostly provided by the twisted human condition- surely the most terrifying of all demons! It often follows a metaphysical thread, blurring dreams and hallucinations with reality- and really commits to it too, which in essence is vital to its' success.

Suspense is king here and at appropriate times it provided a jump, or a dropped a twisted revelation you didn't quite see coming. The moments in between are sprinkled with subtle humour in dialogue and interactions that reminded me of getting the giggles playing games like Final Fanasy IX. The art style is fantastic in my opinion, and the dev clearly has a talent for giving flavour to the environment and characters.

The game also provides one particularly excellent and memorable mind bending spacial/ temporal trippy puzzle sequence that rivals Braid at its very best (drugs, all the drugs).

There isn't much to criticise, but being nitpicky, I found most of the puzzles and inventory items to be a bit too 'neat' and convenient- not an uncommon problem in adventure style games. All of that is forgiven when it throws out some funny dialogue when you try to put some item where it clearly doesn't belong. I love it when a game has a dig at you, the player, for beng dumb or whimsical.

Distraint is a game that tells a story about how greed destroys the soul of its main character, Price. It is a short yet terrifying look at how the guilt and emotions a person may feel from hurting others for their own gain cannot be erased or suppressed. No matter the lip service a person might give to others to compensate for taking advantage of them, the guilt of their conscience will chase them down and kill them. As the scenarios in Distraint show, those most likely to be abused are poor, elderly, or vulnerable in some way. Ultimately, "what goes around comes around." A nice little story with a lesson on morality, set in uniquely terrifying environments.
